lines.text: This is your 20-minute Walk Edition of Walking, part one, by Henry David Thoreau. Start walking. I'll tell you when you're halfway.
lines.speaker: app

lines.text: I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute Freedom and Wildness, as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil,—to regard man as an inhabitant, or a part and parcel of Nature, rather than a member of society.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I wish to make an extreme statement, if so I may make an emphatic one, for there are enough champions of civilization: the minister and the school committee and every one of you will take care of that.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I have met with but one or two persons in the course of my life who understood the art of Walking, that is, of taking walks—who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering, which word is beautifully derived “from idle people who roved about the country, in the Middle Ages, and asked charity, under pretense of going à la Sainte Terre,” to the Holy Land, till the children exclaimed, “There goes a Sainte-Terrer,” a Saunterer, a Holy-Lander.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: They who never go to the Holy Land in their walks, as they pretend, are indeed mere idlers and vagabonds; but they who do go there are saunterers in the good sense, such as I mean.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Some, however, would derive the word from sans terre without land or a home, which, therefore, in the good sense, will mean, having no particular home, but equally at home everywhere.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: For this is the secret of successful sauntering.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: He who sits still in a house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all; but the saunterer, in the good sense, is no more vagrant than the meandering river, which is all the while sedulously seeking the shortest course to the sea.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: But I prefer the first, which, indeed, is the most probable derivation.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: For every walk is a sort of crusade, preached by some Peter the Hermit in us, to go forth and reconquer this Holy Land from the hands of the Infidels.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It is true, we are but faint-hearted crusaders, even the walkers, nowadays, who undertake no persevering, never-ending enterprises.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Our expeditions are but tours, and come round again at evening to the old hearth-side from which we set out.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Half the walk is but retracing our steps.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: We should go forth on the shortest walk, perchance, in the spirit of undying adventure, never to return,—prepared to send back our embalmed hearts only as relics to our desolate kingdoms.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If you are ready to leave father and mother, and brother and sister, and wife and child and friends, and never see them again,—if you have paid your debts, and made your will, and settled all your affairs, and are a free man; then you are ready for a walk.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: To come down to my own experience, my companion and I, for I sometimes have a companion, take pleasure in fancying ourselves knights of a new, or rather an old, order—not Equestrians or Chevaliers, not Ritters or Riders, but Walkers, a still more ancient and honorable class, I trust.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The chivalric and heroic spirit which once belonged to the Rider seems now to reside in, or perchance to have subsided into, the Walker—not the Knight, but Walker Errant.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: He is a sort of fourth estate, outside of Church and State and People.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: We have felt that we almost alone hereabouts practiced this noble art; though, to tell the truth, at least if their own assertions are to be received, most of my townsmen would fain walk sometimes, as I do, but they cannot.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: No wealth can buy the requisite leisure, freedom, and independence which are the capital in this profession.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It comes only by the grace of God.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It requires a direct dispensation from Heaven to become a walker.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: You must be born into the family of the Walkers.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Ambulator nascitur, non fit.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Some of my townsmen, it is true, can remember and have described to me some walks which they took ten years ago, in which they were so blessed as to lose themselves for half an hour in the woods; but I know very well that they have confined themselves to the highway ever since, whatever pretensions they may make to belong to this select class.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: No doubt they were elevated for a moment as by the reminiscence of a previous state of existence, when even they were foresters and outlaws.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: “When he came to grene wode, In a mery mornynge, There he herde the notes small Of byrdes mery syngynge.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: “It is ferre gone, sayd Robyn, That I was last here; Me lyste a lytell for to shote At the donne dere.”
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I think that I cannot preserve my health and spirits, unless I spend four hours a day at least—and it is commonly more than that—sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields, absolutely free from all worldly engagements.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: You may safely say, A penny for your thoughts, or a thousand pounds.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: When sometimes I am reminded that the mechanics and shopkeepers stay in their shops not only all the forenoon, but all the afternoon too, sitting with crossed legs, so many of them—as if the legs were made to sit upon, and not to stand or walk upon—I think that they deserve some credit for not having all committed suicide long ago.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I, who cannot stay in my chamber for a single day without acquiring some rust, and when sometimes I have stolen forth for a walk at the eleventh hour, or four o’clock in the afternoon, too late to redeem the day, when the shades of night were already beginning to be mingled with the daylight, have felt as if I had committed some sin to be atoned for,—I confess that I am astonished at the power of endurance, to say nothing of the moral insensibility, of my neighbors who confine themselves to shops and offices the whole day for weeks and months, aye, and years almost together.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I know not what manner of stuff they are of—sitting there now at three o’clock in the afternoon, as if it were three o’clock in the morning.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Bonaparte may talk of the three-o’clock-in-the-morning courage, but it is nothing to the courage which can sit down cheerfully at this hour in the afternoon over against one’s self whom you have known all the morning, to starve out a garrison to whom you are bound by such strong ties of sympathy.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I wonder that about this time, or say between four and five o’clock in the afternoon, too late for the morning papers and too early for the evening ones, there is not a general explosion heard up and down the street, scattering a legion of antiquated and house-bred notions and whims to the four winds for an airing—and so the evil cure itself.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: How womankind, who are confined to the house still more than men, stand it I do not know; but I have ground to suspect that most of them do not stand it at all.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: When, early in a summer afternoon, we have been shaking the dust of the village from the skirts of our garments, making haste past those houses with purely Doric or Gothic fronts, which have such an air of repose about them, my companion whispers that probably about these times their occupants are all gone to bed.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Then it is that I appreciate the beauty and the glory of architecture, which itself never turns in, but forever stands out and erect, keeping watch over the slumberers.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: No doubt temperament, and, above all, age, have a good deal to do with it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: As a man grows older, his ability to sit still and follow indoor occupations increases.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: He grows vespertinal in his habits as the evening of life approaches, till at last he comes forth only just before sundown, and gets all the walk that he requires in half an hour.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: But the walking of which I speak has nothing in it akin to taking exercise, as it is called, as the sick take medicine at stated hours—as the swinging of dumb-bells or chairs; but is itself the enterprise and adventure of the day.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If you would get exercise, go in search of the springs of life.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Think of a man’s swinging dumb-bells for his health, when those springs are bubbling up in far-off pastures unsought by him!
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Moreover, you must walk like a camel, which is said to be the only beast which ruminates when walking.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: When a traveler asked Wordsworth’s servant to show him her master’s study, she answered, “Here is his library, but his study is out of doors.”
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Living much out of doors, in the sun and wind, will no doubt produce a certain roughness of character—will cause a thicker cuticle to grow over some of the finer qualities of our nature, as on the face and hands, or as severe manual labor robs the hands of some of their delicacy of touch.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: So staying in the house, on the other hand, may produce a softness and smoothness, not to say thinness of skin, accompanied by an increased sensibility to certain impressions.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Perhaps we should be more susceptible to some influences important to our intellectual and moral growth, if the sun had shone and the wind blown on us a little less; and no doubt it is a nice matter to proportion rightly the thick and thin skin.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: You're halfway. If you're walking out and back, turn around now.
lines.speaker: app

lines.text: But methinks that is a scurf that will fall off fast enough—that the natural remedy is to be found in the proportion which the night bears to the day, the winter to the summer, thought to experience.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There will be so much the more air and sunshine in our thoughts.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The callous palms of the laborer are conversant with finer tissues of self-respect and heroism, whose touch thrills the heart, than the languid fingers of idleness.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: That is mere sentimentality that lies abed by day and thinks itself white, far from the tan and callus of experience.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: When we walk, we naturally go to the fields and woods: what would become of us, if we walked only in a garden or a mall?
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Even some sects of philosophers have felt the necessity of importing the woods to themselves, since they did not go to the woods.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: “They planted groves and walks of Platanes,” where they took subdiales ambulationes in porticos open to the air.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Of course it is of no use to direct our steps to the woods, if they do not carry us thither.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I am alarmed when it happens that I have walked a mile into the woods bodily, without getting there in spirit.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: In my afternoon walk I would fain forget all my morning occupations and my obligations to society.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: But it sometimes happens that I cannot easily shake off the village.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The thought of some work will run in my head and I am not where my body is—I am out of my senses.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: In my walks I would fain return to my senses.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What business have I in the woods, if I am thinking of something out of the woods?
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I suspect myself, and cannot help a shudder when I find myself so implicated even in what are called good works—for this may sometimes happen.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: My vicinity affords many good walks; and though for so many years I have walked almost every day, and sometimes for several days together, I have not yet exhausted them.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: An absolutely new prospect is a great happiness, and I can still get this any afternoon.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Two or three hours’ walking will carry me to as strange a country as I expect ever to see.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A single farmhouse which I had not seen before is sometimes as good as the dominions of the king of Dahomey.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There is in fact a sort of harmony discoverable between the capabilities of the landscape within a circle of ten miles’ radius, or the limits of an afternoon walk, and the threescore years and ten of human life.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It will never become quite familiar to you.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Nowadays almost all man’s improvements, so called, as the building of houses and the cutting down of the forest and of all large trees, simply deform the landscape, and make it more and more tame and cheap.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A people who would begin by burning the fences and let the forest stand!
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I saw the fences half consumed, their ends lost in the middle of the prairie, and some worldly miser with a surveyor looking after his bounds, while heaven had taken place around him, and he did not see the angels going to and fro, but was looking for an old post-hole in the midst of paradise.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I looked again, and saw him standing in the middle of a boggy Stygian fen, surrounded by devils, and he had found his bounds without a doubt, three little stones, where a stake had been driven, and looking nearer, I saw that the Prince of Darkness was his surveyor.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I can easily walk ten, fifteen, twenty, any number of miles, commencing at my own door, without going by any house, without crossing a road except where the fox and the mink do: first along by the river, and then the brook, and then the meadow and the wood-side.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There are square miles in my vicinity which have no inhabitant.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: From many a hill I can see civilization and the abodes of man afar.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The farmers and their works are scarcely more obvious than woodchucks and their burrows.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Man and his affairs, church and state and school, trade and commerce, and manufactures and agriculture even politics, the most alarming of them all,—I am pleased to see how little space they occupy in the landscape.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Politics is but a narrow field, and that still narrower highway yonder leads to it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I sometimes direct the traveler thither.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If you would go to the political world, follow the great road,—follow that market-man, keep his dust in your eyes, and it will lead you straight to it; for it, too, has its place merely, and does not occupy all space.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I pass from it as from a bean field into the forest, and it is forgotten.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: In one half hour I can walk off to some portion of the earth’s surface where a man does not stand from one year’s end to another, and there, consequently, politics are not, for they are but as the cigar smoke of a man.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The village is the place to which the roads tend, a sort of expansion of the highway, as a lake of a river.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It is the body of which roads are the arms and legs—a trivial or quadrivial place, the thoroughfare and ordinary of travelers.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The word is from the Latin villa which together with via, a way, or more anciently ved and vella, Varro derives from veho, to carry, because the villa is the place to and from which things are carried.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: They who got their living by teaming were said vellaturam facere.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Hence, too, the Latin word vilis and our vile; also villain.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: This suggests what kind of degeneracy villagers are liable to.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: They are wayworn by the travel that goes by and over them, without traveling themselves.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Some do not walk at all; others walk in the highways; a few walk across lots.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Roads are made for horses and men of business.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I do not travel in them much, comparatively, because I am not in a hurry to get to any tavern or grocery or livery-stable or depot to which they lead.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I am a good horse to travel, but not from choice a roadster.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The landscape-painter uses the figures of men to mark a road.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: He would not make that use of my figure.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I walk out into a nature such as the old prophets and poets, Menu, Moses, Homer, Chaucer, walked in.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: You may name it America, but it is not America: neither Americus Vespucius, nor Columbus, nor the rest were the discoverers of it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There is a truer amount of it in mythology than in any history of America, so called, that I have seen.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: However, there are a few old roads that may be trodden with profit, as if they led somewhere now that they are nearly discontinued.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There is the Old Marlborough Road, which does not go to Marlborough now, methinks, unless that is Marlborough where it carries me.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I am the bolder to speak of it here, because I presume that there are one or two such roads in every town.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: THE OLD MARLBOROUGH ROAD.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Where they once dug for money, But never found any; Where sometimes Martial Miles Singly files, And Elijah Wood, I fear for no good: No other man, Save Elisha Dugan— O man of wild habits, Partridges and rabbits, Who hast no cares Only to set snares, Who liv’st all alone, Close to the bone; And where life is sweetest Constantly eatest.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: When the spring stirs my blood With the instinct to travel, I can get enough gravel On the Old Marlborough Road.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Nobody repairs it, For nobody wears it; It is a living way, As the Christians say.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Not many there be Who enter therein, Only the guests of the Irishman Quin.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What is it, what is it But a direction out there, And the bare possibility Of going somewhere?
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Great guide boards of stone, But travelers none; Cenotaphs of the towns Named on their crowns.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It is worth going to see Where you might be.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What king Did the thing, I am still wondering; Set up how or when, By what selectmen, Gourgas or Lee, Clark or Darby?
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: They’re a great endeavor To be something forever; Blank tablets of stone, Where a traveler might groan, And in one sentence Grave all that is known Which another might read, In his extreme need.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I know one or two Lines that would do, Literature that might stand All over the land, Which a man could remember Till next December, And read again in the spring, After the thawing.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If with fancy unfurled You leave your abode, You may go round the world By the Old Marlborough Road.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: At present, in this vicinity, the best part of the land is not private property; the landscape is not owned, and the walker enjoys comparative freedom.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: But possibly the day will come when it will be partitioned off into so-called pleasure grounds, in which a few will take a narrow and exclusive pleasure only,—when fences shall be multiplied, and man traps and other engines invented to confine men to the public road, and walking over the surface of God’s earth shall be construed to mean trespassing on some gentleman’s grounds.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: To enjoy a thing exclusively is commonly to exclude yourself from the true enjoyment of it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Let us improve our opportunities, then, before the evil days come.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Here is something to think about on the way back. If the true spirit of walking is to be like the meandering river seeking the sea, what does that suggest about the purpose of your own journey?
lines.speaker: app

lines.text: That's the end. You should be almost home.
